nameStory: This bee honors Dru Drury, an 18th-century English entomologist who was one of the first to scientifically document insects from the Americas. The 'long-horned' part refers to the males' impressively lengthy antennae, which can be nearly as long as their entire body and give them an almost alien appearance.
description: Drury's Long-horned Bee is a medium-sized native bee about the size of a honeybee, with females typically being more robust than males. The most striking feature is found on males - their extraordinarily long, thread-like antennae that seem almost comically oversized. Both sexes have a somewhat fuzzy, rustic appearance with muted brown and amber coloring, earning them their alternate name of 'rustic longhorn bee'. These solitary bees are important pollinators that you might spot visiting late-summer flowers.

idTips.label: Male Antennae
idTips.description: Males have remarkably long, thin antennae that extend well beyond their head - almost cartoon-like in their length and constantly moving as they feed

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Overall rusty brown to amber coloration with a somewhat matte, fuzzy texture rather than the shiny appearance of many other bees

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Medium-sized, similar to a honeybee but stockier, with females noticeably more robust and rounded than the slender males

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Males fly with a distinctive hovering, darting motion around flowers, their long antennae visible even in flight

idTips.label: Flower Preference
idTips.description: Often seen on late-season flowers like goldenrod and asters, where they feed with their antennae constantly twitching

habitat: Look for Drury's Long-horned Bees in open areas with abundant late-summer wildflowers, including meadows, field edges, roadsides, and prairie-like habitats. They prefer sunny locations with native flowers like goldenrod, asters, and sunflowers. The females nest in the ground, often choosing sandy or well-drained soil in sparsely vegetated areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active yet - they're still developing underground in their nest cells from the previous year.
seasonality.summer: Late summer is peak time, with adults emerging in July and August when their preferred flowers are blooming.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall as they complete mating and females prepare nest sites for next year's generation.
seasonality.winter: No adults visible - the species overwinters as developing larvae in underground nest cells.

funFact: The male's extremely long antennae aren't just for show - they're packed with scent receptors that can detect a female's pheromones from remarkable distances, essentially turning each antenna into a super-sensitive chemical radar system for finding mates.
confusionNotes: The long antennae make males unmistakable, but females can be confused with other brown, fuzzy bees. Look for their preference for late-season flowers and their rustic, matte appearance rather than the shinier look of many other bee species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'long-horned bee,' the long appendages are antennae, not horns - true horns are found on mammals, while insects have antennae for sensing their environment. The Melissodes genus includes many species that are specialized pollinators of fall-blooming plants.
compareHints: Among its Melissodes relatives, Drury's Long-horned Bee is distinguished by its rustic brown coloration and preference for a wide variety of late-season flowers. The Common Longhorn Bee tends to be more golden-yellow, while the Two-spotted Longhorn Bee has distinctive light spots on its abdomen that Drury's lacks. The males of all Melissodes species have long antennae, but Drury's tends to have a more muted, brownish appearance overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the nine other Melissodes species in New England, the Two-spotted Longhorn Bee is distinguished primarily by those diagnostic pale spots.

Among its Melissodes relatives, the Dark-veined Longhorn Bee stands out for having the most conspicuous dark wing veins - while Common Longhorn Bees and Two-spotted Longhorn Bees have similar body shapes and fuzzy appearance, their wing veins are typically lighter and less noticeable.

Eastern Thistle Longhorn Bees are best distinguished from their Melissodes cousins by their timing and flower preferences - they're active later in summer than most relatives and show a strong preference for thistle flowers.
Among its longhorn bee relatives, the Denticulate Longhorn Bee is most reliably distinguished by its strong association with ironweed flowers rather than physical features alone.
